props.title: Zero for Conduct

sections.content: Zero for Conduct (1933) revolutionized rebellious youth cinema with its surreal, anarchic portrayal of boarding school uprising. Director Jean Vigo, drawing from his own harsh school experiences, created a dreamlike manifesto of childhood rebellion that directly influenced François Truffaut's The 400 Blows (1959) and Lindsay Anderson's If.... (1968). The film's most famous sequence - the slow-motion dormitory pillow fight - became a blueprint for depicting youthful freedom, while its anti-authoritarian spirit echoes through countless school rebellion films like Dead Poets Society (1989) and The Breakfast Club (1985). sections.content: Vigo's radical approach to depicting childhood merged documentary-style realism with poetic surrealism, creating a new cinematic language that influenced the French New Wave. The film's brief 44-minute runtime packs remarkable power, with compositions that transform mundane school settings into dreamlike spaces of resistance. The influence extends to modern works like The White Ribbon (2009) and The Devil's Backbone (2001), which similarly explore the dark undercurrents of childhood institutions.

The film's treatment of authority figures as grotesque caricatures established a template followed by works like Pink Floyd: The Wall (1982) and Rushmore (1998). Vigo's use of nonprofessional child actors and natural performances anticipated the neo-realist movement and continues to influence contemporary youth-centered cinema like The Florida Project (2017) and System Crasher (2019). sections.content: Though banned upon release, Zero for Conduct became a cornerstone of counterculture cinema. Its DNA is visible in everything from Jean-Luc Godard's Band of Outsiders (1964) to Lucile Hadžihalilović's Innocence (2004). The film's blend of realism and fantasy particularly influenced Latin American directors like Guillermo del Toro, whose Pan's Labyrinth (2006) shares its ability to capture childhood's simultaneous wonder and terror.
